subject: Align on initial payload SLO and streaming format decision
messages:
From: Camila Reyes <camila@redwood.com>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>

Subject: Align on initial payload SLO and streaming format decision

Thanks again for taking the call earlier, Samir and Priya — great to hear more about AveryTech's real-time summarization use case. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have alignment before the pilot kicks off.

Recap / what you told us
- Traffic: ~120–220 RPS during peak windows, spiky bursts to ~400 RPS for short periods.
- Current client: WebSocket-based streaming aggregator. Prefer to keep websocket if it avoids extra infra work.
- Success metrics: minimize perceived latency in the product; objective is a snappy first update in the UI.

Redwood proposal (initially scoped)
- TTFT goal (proposal): 99th percentile <= 200 ms end-to-end in-app (we'll propose two measurement lenses below).
- Measurement lenses:
  1) "Server-first-byte" TTFT: time from request arrival at runtime to first token emitted (recommended for benchmarking).
  2) "Client-first-update" TTFT: time from client request/ACK to UI paint (captures network+client).
- Streaming mode: we can support both SSE and WebSocket. For AveryTech's short messages and existing WS investment, I suggest WebSocket primary + SSE as fallback for troubleshooting.
- Chunk cadence: target 1–3 chunks per 200 ms window for typical responses (helps maintain UI fluidity without tiny micro-chunks).
- Concurrency: plan for sustained 200 concurrent requests with capacity to burst to 400 for up to 30s; autoscale policy during pilot will be set accordingly.

Asks / next steps
1) Please share a representative 15-minute sample trace (we can use the Drive link) or a small synthetic generator (format in attached sheet).
2) Decide which TTFT lens you want us to emphasize in reports (server-first-byte vs client-first-update).
3) Quick engineering sync: 30 minutes to go over auth, chunk boundaries, and heartbeat/keepalive behavior. Proposed windows: Wed 5/27 9:00–9:30 PT or Thu 5/28 11:00–11:30 PT.

Attachments: pilot-slos.xlsx (pilot SLO proposal + measurement templates), sse-vs-ws-demo-recording.mp4 (short demo we ran for a similar customer).

Thanks — I can get Ben (runtime lead) involved for the sync to cover kernel/kv cache priming details.

— Camila

Thanks Camila — this is very helpful. A few clarifying q's before the sync: 

1) Measurement: when you say "server-first-byte" TTFT, does that exclude network latency entirely? Our internal dashboards measure from the client SDK call to first UI update, which adds ~40–70 ms on average across our regions. We want the reported customer-facing TTFT to reflect real user experience unless you recommend separating the two.

2) WebSocket specifics: we currently send a small handshake payload (10–20 bytes) then stream chunks as they arrive. How do you handle chunk framing for partial JSON objects? We need clear rules on whether Redwood will emit chunk-delimited JSON messages or send length-prefixed frames.

3) Auth / keepalives: our clients like long-lived WS connections. Any constraints on token TTLs or session refresh patterns to avoid dropped requests mid-response?

Proposed sync: Wed 5/27 9:00 PT works for our engs. I've attached a short Wireshark-like trace in the Drive folder (traffic/sample-trace.json). I'll loop in our infra lead if needed.

Samir — thanks for the questions, happy to clarify ahead of the sync. Short answers and proposed defaults below.

1) TTFT measurement (our recommendation)- For bench reporting, we present both:
   • server-first-byte: time from request reaching Redwood runtime (post-load-balancer) to first token emitted. This isolates runtime performance and is repeatable for piloting + tuning.
   • client-first-update: we can instrument your SDK to capture end-to-end time. We will provide both metrics side-by-side and call out network/diff.

2) Chunk framing and partial JSON- Default: Redwood emits application/json stream frames where each chunk is a valid JSON token sequence if the model output is structured. For your existing flow, we can instead use length-prefixed frames over WebSocket (we support both) so your aggregator can reconstruct objects deterministically. We'll avoid splitting a JSON object across more than 2 small frames unless the tokenization forces it. We'll document exact framing rules in the sync.

3) Auth / token TTLs- Long-lived WS connections are supported. We recommend JWTs with a 6-hour TTL for sessions and a short-lived request token (1–2 minutes) for individual calls if you plan to reuse connections for many requests. Our SDK supports auto-refresh; if you prefer to manage refreshes in-house, we can share the refresh hook.

4) KV cache priming / cold starts- For predictable TTFT, we recommend priming commonly used system prompts in a warm cache before peak windows. We'll include a warmup script in the pilot SLO workbook.

Pilot plan (high-level)
- Day 0: ingest sample traffic + baseline server-first-byte measurements at 50 RPS.
- Day 1: ramp to sustained 200 RPS, capture 50/95/99 percentiles, iterate on chunk cadence.
- Day 2: burst tests to 400 RPS for 30s windows.

Attachments referenced: pilot-slos.xlsx (sheet: measurement-plan), sse-vs-ws-demo-recording.mp4. I'll be on the sync to walk through framing and runtime knobs.

— Ben
